newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore October exports show glimmer of light.
newsitem.headline: Singapore October exports show glimmer of light.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil exports rose marginally in October after two consecutive months of sharp declines, trade figures showed on Wednesday, leading economists to forecast a slow but gradual improvement for business.
Non-oil exports rose a nominal 1.1 percent year-on-year in October against a 6.2 percent fall in September and a 6.3 percent fall in August, the Trade Development Board.

"It is a little softer than what we were expecting, but it is still in line with our expectations for an improvement in the exports growth figures over fourth quarter," said Desmond Supple, senior emerging markets economist with I.D.E.A.
"This supports anecdoctal evidence we have seen that the worst of the decline in external demand for electronics goods is over now and we are expecting gradual firming in business conditions."
Singapore's exports had slumped over the last six months due to a slowdown in the electronics industry in the United States and Japan.
Electronics, computers and related products account for about half of the island's total industrial production and almost 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
The dependence on the electronics industry had dragged Singapore's gross domestic product growth down to 3.2 percent in the third quarter, from 11.4 percent in the first three months of the year.
"The trade figures were slightly better than we expected, but not surprising," said Ng Bok Eng, regional economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
However, he said it would be premature to say the data signalled a turning point in Singapore's economic slowdown.
"We are not likely to see a very sharp pick-up in export growth over the next two to three months," Ng said.
The trade board said exports of disk drives, integrated circuits and microcomputers to the United States, Singapore's main trading partner, were higher in October.
"This is in line with expectations that the global electronic cycle has bottomed and is beginning to filter through into Singapore's electronic sector," said an analyst for Crosby Securities.
Overall non-oil domestic exports to the United States decrerased by 3.3 percent to S$2.2 billion in October, based on a three-month moving average percentage change, the trade board said.
Economists said October's industrial production figure, due out early next month, would be closely watched for confirmation that electronics is on the road to recovery.
Daniel Lian, a regional economist with NatWest Markets, said he would be watching inventory and production levels.
The analyst with Crosby Securities said the November exports figure might show a decline because of strong exports in November of last year.
Economists were also cautious about the continued weakness in retained imports -- which looks at imports after deducting re-exports -- a leading indicator for the manufacturing sector.
"Lower retained imports means manufacturers are not importing raw materials and components, which suggest in the short-term, conditions are likely to remain quite difficult," Ng said.
